newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds strengthen amid talk of Irish rates cut.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds strengthen amid talk of Irish rates cut.

text.p: Irish bonds continued to strengthen in active late trade on Tuesday amid speculation of possible cut in Irish interest rates.

"All the action is very much concentrated on the shorter end of the market. The Irish Central Bank was apparently in the market earlier taking cash out in the one-month money rate area," one dealer said.

By 1555 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was up 20 pence from Monday's close at 103.50 to yield 5.62 percent while the key benchmark eight percent bond due 2006 was up 45 pence from the close at 111.05 to yield 6.40 percent.
Dealers said Irish bonds were trading 112 basis points over German bunds in the five-year area and 86 basis points over Germany in the 10-year area.
The one-month money rate was at 5.56/.69 compared to 5.63/.75 at the previous close.

Earlier, Ireland's National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) said that it would auction 150 million punts of the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 in a competitive auction for primary dealers on February 18.
Up to 30 million punts of the stock will also be offered in a non-competitive auction, the NTMA said.

Dealers said developments in the Irish market over-shadowed events elsewhere, including the U.S. where the Treasury is to issue three, 10 and 30-year bonds worth a total of $39.75 billion dollars at the quarterly auctions.

The auctions, scheduled for Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, will see the issue of $17.75 billion dollars of three-year notes, $12.0 billion of 10-year notes and $10.0 billion of 30-year bonds respectively.
Corporate bond high-grade debt issuance will take a back seat as the U.S. Treasury's quarterly refunding gets underway, U.S. dealers said.
